opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the clearest cases where AI could deliver enormous, broadly shared benefits fairly soon. Most people in the world don't have reliable access to a good doctor, and even in wealthy countries, getting expert attention is slow, expensive, and often rushed. You might get ten minutes with a physician who's seen dozens of patients that day. An AI system that can take a careful history, ask good follow-up questions, explain things patiently, and draw on the whole medical literature could be transformative, especially for people who currently get no expert advice at all.

There's also early evidence that these systems can perform quite well on diagnostic reasoning, sometimes comparably to clinicians on certain benchmarks. They're also often rated as more empathetic, partly because they have unlimited time and don't get tired or irritated. That combination of competence and patience is unusual.

From a governance perspective, I also find it promising as a model domain. Medicine already has institutions for evaluation, liability, licensing, and post-deployment monitoring. So it's a place where we can learn how to responsibly integrate highly capable AI into high-stakes decisions: how to validate performance, handle errors, keep humans appropriately in the loop, and build justified trust instead of blind trust or reflexive rejection.

Of course there are real risks: overconfidence, hallucination, uneven performance across populations, privacy, and the question of who's accountable when things go wrong. But I think the upside is large enough that we should try hard to get this right rather than either rushing it or blocking it.

r002.rationale: It notes that access to doctors is slow and discusses keeping humans involved, but does not explain that AI guidance on when to see a doctor would help use doctors’ time more effectively.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the thing that excites me most is the potential to dramatically expand access. Right now, if you think about it, the vast majority of the world's population has very limited access to high-quality medical expertise. Even in wealthy countries, you often wait weeks to see a specialist, you get maybe fifteen minutes of their time, and they're working with incomplete information about your history. And in low-income countries, the ratio of doctors to patients can be orders of magnitude worse.

So one promising vision is that AI systems could provide something like a first-line consultation to anyone with a phone — something that's patient, that has read essentially the entire medical literature, that can ask follow-up questions, that doesn't get tired at the end of a long shift. Even if it's not as good as the best human physician, the relevant comparison for billions of people isn't the best human physician, it's nothing, or a long delay, or a search engine.

I'd also say there's something interesting about the epistemics here. Humans have well-documented biases in diagnosis — anchoring on the first hypothesis, availability bias, that sort of thing. AI systems have their own failure modes, of course, and we should be very cautious about those. But there's at least the possibility of a system that considers a broader differential, that flags rare conditions a generalist might miss, and that could complement human judgment rather than replace it.

That said, I want to be careful. I'm not a medical professional, and I think the governance questions here are hard. How do you ensure these systems are reliable, how do you handle liability when they get things wrong, how do you make sure they're actually deployed where they'd do the most good rather than just adding convenience for people who already have good access? Those questions matter a lot, and I think the promise only gets realised if we take them seriously. But the underlying opportunity — making expert-level medical reasoning something close to a public good — strikes me as one of the clearest near-term benefits of this technology.

astra-6.text:
What I find promising is the possibility of giving everyone access to good medical advice at very low cost. If you’re worried about a symptom, you could have a conversation with a system that has the time to ask follow-up questions, explain the possibilities, and help you decide whether you need to see a doctor urgently or whether it’s reasonable to wait.

And that could be particularly valuable for people who currently have very little access to healthcare. The relevant comparison for them may be getting no advice at all.

Of course, you need to establish that these systems are reliable. A fluent, reassuring answer can be harmful if it’s wrong. But if we can make them appropriately cautious and good at recognising when to involve a clinician, there’s an enormous opportunity to make medical expertise more accessible.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing I find promising is the possibility of giving everyone access to patient, high-quality medical advice at very low cost. You could describe your symptoms, ask follow-up questions, and have someone help you understand what might be going on and whether you need to seek care. And you could do that in your own language, at any time of day.

The challenge is making sure the system is reliable and knows when to defer to a clinician. But if we can get that right, this could be especially valuable for people who currently have very little access to medical expertise. It could also help doctors by gathering information before a consultation and helping patients understand and follow through on their advice.
